processing: Fully oxidised orthodox black tea, sold both in bulk and as a whole-leaf single-estate pack.
harvest_season: No garden-specific calendar is documented; as with other Assam gardens, the May to June second flush is generally the most valued.
appearance_dry: Dark whole leaf with golden tips, as is usual for a good Assam orthodox.
appearance_liquor: Clear reddish amber, typical of Assam orthodox.
taste_profile: Malty and rounded, with less astringency than many Assam orthodox teas according to its sellers.

brewing.notes: Whole leaf takes a little longer than broken grades. Try it plain first, since softness is its selling point.

vintage_note: Goes out both as bulk orthodox for export and as branded single-estate packs from Goodricke. Season is not always stated on the retail pack, so check the packing date; like other Assam black teas, it is best within a year or two.
description:
Harmutty is a Goodricke estate in the Lakhimpur area, placed by its sellers on the bank of the Dikrong river, with the Arunachal hills to the north. Its orthodox tea has long gone into bulk trade, and only recently has it had a retail face of its own.

The tea is orthodox, so it keeps its leaf shape instead of being cut into CTC granules. That usually means a slower, clearer steep than the strong granular teas sold across much of Assam.

Sellers describe a malty, rounded cup that is gentler than many Assam orthodox teas; that is their description, not an independent tasting. Give it three to four minutes and taste it without milk before deciding whether it needs any.

Buying is simple, because the single-estate pack carries the garden name directly. Look for the packing date.
history:
Goodricke's own page says the garden was founded in 1878, while a 2014 trade blog says 1870. Goodricke's Assam orthodox teas from Nonaipara, Harmutty, Orangajuli and Dejoo have been sold in bulk to buyers in the Middle East, the UK and Germany.

In March 2023, Harmutty became one of four gardens behind Goodricke's Assam single-estate brands, launched for the 200th anniversary of the Assam tea industry. That made the name visible to ordinary shoppers.
